analysis.body:
The most concrete public record of AI deployment across the United States federal government comes from the Government Accountability Office, which found that twenty of twenty-three major agencies reported approximately 1,200 current and planned AI use cases. However, per the GAO, most of those use cases were still in the planning phase rather than in production, and only in about 200 instances were agencies actually using AI at the time of review. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of use cases. Reported applications included analyzing drone photography, processing large datasets, identifying border activities through camera and radar feeds, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, suggesting that operational deployment is concentrated in data-intensive and sensor-driven functions rather than general administration.

The GAO's findings on compliance and data quality temper any optimistic reading of those inventory numbers. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each of their reported use cases, while fifteen had instances of incomplete or inaccurate data. Two agencies even included uses that were later determined not to be AI at all. On the requirements side, only ten of the twenty-three agencies reviewed had implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve had implemented some but not all, and the Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI. Per the GAO, without such guidance agencies cannot consistently manage AI, and without accurate inventories the government's management of its AI use will be hindered.

The fiscal dimension is visible in part: the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI, according to the GAO. Operationally, agencies are using AI to identify information security threats and facilitate the review of large datasets, among other uses. The General Services Administration established an AI Center of Excellence, and the Department of Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards, representing two of the more fully implemented structural requirements identified in the GAO review.

Internationally, Oxford Insights publishes the Government AI Readiness Index, which scores nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption and serves as the standard cross-national comparison for where governments stand relative to one another. The OECD.AI Policy Observatory complements that picture by tracking national AI strategies, public-sector initiatives, and ethical frameworks across member and partner countries, with access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives. Stanford HAI's annual AI Index carries the government and policy track, covering legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, and its 2026 edition notes a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it.

The legislative environment is moving rapidly and in many directions at once. Theworldofai.org tracks 2,427 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily, giving a live view of the regulatory surface that federal agencies and their vendors must anticipate. The OECD has articulated AI principles oriented toward trustworthy, transparent, and rights-respecting systems, and the GPAI initiative joined forces with OECD member countries' work on AI under a unified brand in July 2024. For any organization deciding whether to deploy AI in or alongside government, the practical implication of the GAO record is that compliance infrastructure, accurate use-case documentation, and clear acquisition guidance are not yet settled, making governance readiness at least as important a planning variable as the technology itself.
